summary: Sirach 28 warns that vengeance and anger damage the one who holds them and stand in tension with asking the Lord for mercy. The chapter then turns to quarrels, slander, and the tongue, picturing speech as fire, weapon, trap, and burden. It ends by urging readers to guard words as carefully as property or money.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers one of Sirach’s central concerns: wisdom is tested in how a person handles anger, conflict, and speech. It shows that covenant faithfulness is not abstract; it reaches into grudges, arguments, listening, and speaking.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish audiences who wanted instruction for living according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly dated to 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem and the wider Jewish world under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, Torah study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings, using direct commands, vivid comparisons, and repeated warnings about conduct.

outline.heading: Vengeance and Forgiveness
outline.note: The chapter begins by opposing vengeance, anger, and wrath to forgiveness, prayer, remembrance of death, the commandments, and the covenant.

outline.heading: Strife as Fire
outline.note: The teacher warns against strife, showing how anger and hasty contention can grow like a fire or be quenched by what comes from the mouth.

outline.heading: The Damage of Slander
outline.note: The chapter curses the whisperer and double-tongued, then describes slander as socially destructive and more deadly than physical blows.

outline.heading: Sheltered from the Tongue
outline.note: The teacher calls someone happy who is kept from the tongue’s power, then pictures it as an iron yoke, a deadly force, and a flame that overtakes those who forsake the Lord.

outline.heading: Guarding the Mouth
outline.note: The closing image urges the reader to secure words as carefully as possessions, lest speech cause a dangerous fall.

keyVerses.text: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter’s opening concern most directly: forgiveness of a neighbor and seeking pardon from God are held together.

keyVerses.text: If you blow on a spark, it will burn; and if you spit upon it, it will be quenched. Both of these come out of your mouth.
keyVerses.why: This image anchors the middle of the chapter, where speech can inflame conflict or put it out.

keyVerses.text: The stroke of a whip makes a mark in the flesh, but the stroke of a tongue will break bones.
keyVerses.why: The verse gives the chapter’s strongest comparison between physical injury and the damage caused by destructive speech.

keyVerses.text: so make a balance and a weight for your words, and make a door and a bar for your mouth.
keyVerses.why: The closing command turns the warnings into a practical image: words should be weighed and the mouth guarded.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with vengeance?
questions.answer: The opening warns that a person who takes vengeance will also face vengeance from the Lord. The chapter immediately connects this with forgiveness, prayer, anger, mercy, and sins. Its point is not a legal theory of every case but a wisdom warning against nursing retaliation while asking God for pardon.

questions.question: Does verse 2 mean forgiveness earns pardon automatically?
questions.answer: The verse says, “Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done,” and then speaks of sins being pardoned when one prays. In the flow of the chapter, the teacher is exposing the contradiction of asking mercy from the Lord while refusing mercy to another human being. Readers differ on how to relate this to later doctrines of forgiveness, but the chapter itself stresses moral consistency in prayer and neighborly conduct.

questions.question: What does “being flesh” add to the warning?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says the angry person is “flesh” and yet nourishes wrath. In this chapter, that points to human frailty: the person who needs atonement still feeds anger against another. The next verse reinforces that perspective by telling the reader to remember death and corruption.

questions.question: Why does remembering death help stop enmity?
questions.answer: The chapter tells the reader to remember the “last end,” “corruption and death,” and the commandments. That memory puts quarrels inside the limits of mortal life and covenant obligation. The instruction is practical wisdom: do not let anger rule as though life and accountability were endless abstractions.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe strife?
questions.answer: Strife is pictured as something that can be kindled like a fire. A passionate person “will kindle strife,” and hasty contention can lead to bloodshed. The images emphasize escalation: a quarrel may begin small but grow through anger and speech.

questions.question: Who are the “whisperer” and “double-tongued”?
questions.answer: The chapter groups them with the slanderer and treats them as people whose speech destroys peace. “Double-tongued” suggests divided or deceptive speech, while “whisperer” points to damaging speech spread quietly. The text focuses less on defining their psychology and more on the social wreckage their words cause.

questions.question: Is the chapter exaggerating when it says the tongue kills more than the sword?
questions.answer: Verse 18 uses a sharp comparison: many fall by the sword, but more fall because of the tongue. This is wisdom poetry, so the line works by forceful comparison rather than by giving a statistic. The surrounding verses show what kind of damage is meant: broken bodies, displaced people, ruined households, unrest, and loss of peace.

questions.question: What is Hades doing in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 21 says the tongue’s death is so evil that “Hades is better than it.” In this English rendering, Hades names the realm of the dead. The comparison is severe and poetic, underscoring how unbearable and destructive malicious speech can be.

questions.question: What does it mean to make “a balance and a weight” for words?
questions.answer: The closing image compares guarded speech to protecting possessions and measuring valuable goods. A balance and weight suggest careful evaluation before speaking, while a door and bar suggest restraint. The chapter ends by making speech a matter of deliberate discipline, not impulse.

glossary.def: Retaliation or payback. The chapter warns that taking vengeance brings the person under the Lord’s judgment rather than freeing the person from wrong.
Another person in ordinary social life, especially the one who has caused hurt in verse 2. The chapter tests prayer and forgiveness in relation to this nearby person.
Conflict or quarrel. In this chapter it is something anger can kindle and wise restraint can diminish.
A person whose damaging speech harms others. The chapter describes the slanderer as shaking communities, separating people, and ruining peace.
A figure for speech. Sirach 28 pictures it as able to wound, trap, burn, and destroy when not guarded.
